bindings.claim: Gateway routes POST /links to the link service, which dedupes by a client Idempotency-Key (or alias/content hash) before inserting the immutable mapping into Links DB, rejecting alias collisions with 409; it then write-through populates Redis so the first redirect is already a cache hit.

GET /{code} resolves via gateway and link service against Redis; on a cache miss it reads the hot standby replica, and if the replica lacks the row (lag) or is unreachable it falls through to the primary directly, so a just-created link or a replica outage never produces a false miss. The click event gets a synchronous ack and retry before the 302 returns.

The dashboard query goes through gateway and link service to the decoupled Click Counts Store, refreshed by a 12-way partitioned aggregator every 30s from the click-event queue — well inside the 5-minute bound — with idempotent upserts and monitoring watching backlog and lag.

Corrected hop budget: hit path gateway5+service10+cache5+clickAck2=22ms; cache-miss-to-replica adds 15ms (37ms, including the failed 5ms cache lookup); the rare replica-miss-to-primary adds 10ms more (47ms) — every path stays under the 50ms p99 budget.

Redirects now have a two-tier DB fallback: replica first, then primary directly if the replica is behind or down, so no single Postgres instance is the sole in-line dependency; after a promotion, automated reprovisioning rebuilds a fresh standby within minutes, restoring the two-tier shape.

Click events get a synchronous, acknowledged, retried enqueue (no silent loss) and a 12-way partitioned aggregator batches them every 30s with idempotent dedup; monitoring alerts on queue backlog or aggregator lag before the 5-minute bound is ever at risk.
Links DB is a single Postgres instance indexed on short code; 20 million rows is well within one instance's capacity with headroom before sharding would ever be needed.

At 2,000 rps average, nearly all reads hit the write-through cache; residual misses go to the replica, and only a replica outage or lag falls through to the primary — average load never depends on one unreplicated Postgres instance, and corrected hop math (22/37/47ms) still clears 50ms.

At 10,000 rps peak the cache serves the bulk of reads, the replica (sized for 100% of peak) and primary form a two-tier read fallback with no sole SPOF, and the click pipeline is a 12-partition consumer group sized to the same 10k events/sec peak so the aggregator never backs up.

narrative.overview: This revision closes the SPOF the panel found twice: a cache miss used to have exactly one fallback, the hot replica, with no further fallback and no story for after it's promoted. Now a cache miss tries the replica first and, only if the replica lacks the row — the lag window right after a create — or is unreachable, falls through to the primary, so a just-created link can't 404 and no single Postgres instance is ever the sole in-line dependency. After a promotion, automated reprovisioning rebuilds a fresh standby within minutes so the two-tier fallback survives more than one failure a month. The click event that used to be fire-and-forget now gets a synchronous broker ack and bounded retry (~2ms) before the redirect returns, with an explicit alert if retries are exhausted — loss is observed, never silent. The aggregator is now a stated 12-way consumer group, partitioned to match the 10,000 events/sec peak, so a single-consumer bottleneck can't back the freshness bound up at the worst moment. Monitoring now also watches queue backlog and aggregator lag. I corrected the hop-budget arithmetic to include the failed cache lookup on every miss path (22ms hit / 37ms replica-fallback / 47ms double-fallback, all under 50ms) and added idempotency-key dedup plus an alias-collision check to create.

componentRationales.prose: The marketer and the visitor are the same client surface: one issues creates and reads the dashboard, the other just follows redirects. No change requested here.

Still a thin router with a declared 5ms hop budget and metrics emission. createLink is now explicitly idempotent — it honors a client Idempotency-Key so a retried POST can't silently create two links for one submission.

Owns create and redirect logic with a fully explicit interface: cache read/populate, DB write-create (deduped by idempotency key, alias-collision checked), a two-tier read fallback (replica, then primary when the replica is behind or down), a synchronous acknowledged-and-retried click emit, and counts read. No operation does double duty, and no redirect can silently fail or silently lose its click.
Still write-through on create, no TTL needed since mappings never change. Unchanged beyond that — the panel's findings were about the fallback chain behind it, not the cache itself.

Primary system of record for the immutable mapping. It's also now the tier-2 fallback for any redirect the replica can't serve — a just-created link, or any read while the replica is down — and the endpoint is logical: after a promotion, whichever instance holds the primary role answers here without a new edge.

A hot standby sized for 100% of peak, serving as tier-1 fallback and promotion target — but no longer the sole fallback, since the primary now backs it up on the same path. After a promotion, automated reprovisioning rebuilds a fresh standby within minutes, so the two-tier shape survives more than one failure a month.

A durable, at-least-once log, now partitioned 12 ways so a single consumer can't become the bottleneck at peak. It's also now written to synchronously with a broker ack, not fired-and-forgotten, so a failed enqueue is retried rather than silently dropped.

Now modeled as a 12-member consumer group, one per partition, explicitly sized to the 10,000 events/sec peak — the single-consumer bottleneck can't recur. Idempotent, keyed upserts still guard against double-counting on retry or hot-key contention.
Unchanged: the counter lives here, fully decoupled from the immutable link row.

Now also watches queue backlog and aggregator consumer lag, not just gateway/cache/DB/replica latency — a stalled aggregator or a backing-up queue is caught before the 5-minute freshness bound is at risk. It also raises an explicit alert if a click event's retries are exhausted, so a lost click is observed rather than silently absorbed.

criterionNarrations.prose: Create still goes gateway→service→single immutable insert, but now dedupes a retried submission by idempotency key and rejects a colliding custom alias with 409 before the insert, so a flaky client can't silently fork a second link for one request.

Redirect is still cache-first with a replica fallback, but the replica fallback now itself falls through to the primary when the replica lacks the row — exactly the window right after a create — or is unreachable, so the promised redirect no longer has a window where it 404s, and the click event is acknowledged and retried rather than fired-and-forgotten.

The marketer's click count comes from a 12-way partitioned aggregator sized to peak, writing idempotent upserts into a store decoupled from the link row; monitoring now also watches queue backlog and aggregator lag so a stall is caught, not just assumed away.

Corrected hop math: hit path is 22ms (gateway5+service10+cache5+click-ack2); a replica fallback is 37ms once the failed 5ms cache lookup is counted; the rare replica-miss-to-primary path is 47ms. All three clear the 50ms p99 budget with headroom.

The in-line redirect path now has two independent DB tiers — replica, then primary — so neither alone is a sole SPOF, and automated reprovisioning rebuilds the standby within minutes of a promotion, restoring the two-tier shape before a second failure is likely in the same month.

Click events are acknowledged and retried on enqueue (no silent loss), aggregated by a 12-way consumer group sized to the 10,000/sec peak, and monitoring now alerts on queue backlog or aggregator lag directly — freshness is observed, not just asserted from the 30s interval.

Links DB is a single Postgres instance indexed on short code; 20 million rows is well within one instance's capacity with headroom before sharding would ever be needed — unaffected by this round's fallback-chain changes.

At 2,000 rps average the cache absorbs nearly all reads; a replica-then-primary fallback chain, both correctly sized, means no single unreplicated instance sits in-line, and the corrected hop math (22/37/47ms) still clears the latency budget comfortably.

At 10,000 rps peak the same cache-plus-two-tier-DB shape holds for reads, and the click pipeline is now an explicit 12-partition consumer group matched to that same peak rate, so the aggregator can't back up at exactly the load where it matters most.
Links are inserted once via dbWriteCreate (now idempotent) and never updated; no edge or operation in the graph performs an update to a link row, consistent with the immutability constraint.
